desc:
In the m x n matrix grid, every row and every column is sorted in non-decreasing order. Values may repeat.

For each value q in queries (in order), count how many cells of grid hold a value less than or equal to q. Return the list of counts, one per query. Each query should be answered without looking at every cell.
constraints: Each row and each column is in non-decreasing order
hints: A single query can be answered by counting in each row separately: in a sorted row, the cells ≤ q form a prefix, whose length a binary search finds.
The columns are sorted too, so the length of that prefix can only shrink as you move down the rows. You can walk one pointer instead of searching each row.

Start in the bottom-left corner. If the current cell is greater than q, move up. Otherwise the cells above it in this column are all ≤ q: add row + 1 and move right. Repeat until you leave the grid; this is O(m + n) per query.
editorial: Fix one query q. The cells with value ≤ q form a 'staircase' region anchored at the top-left corner, because both rows and columns are sorted. Counting its cells means finding, for each column, how many cells from the top are ≤ q.

Walk the boundary of that region from the bottom-left corner. If grid[row][col] > q, this cell and everything below it in the column are too big, so move up. Otherwise this cell and everything above it in the column are ≤ q, so add row + 1 to the answer and move right to the next column. The walk moves up at most m times and right at most n times, so a query costs O(m + n).

Total cost is O(Q * (m + n)). Binary searching every row instead gives O(Q * m log n), which is also acceptable but slower for tall grids. This 'count the cells not exceeding a value' routine is exactly the counting step used by the k-th smallest in a sorted matrix binary search.
